content: The prevalence of physical impairments among children and adolescents in Western countries is high and continues to rise. Many nations provide personal assistance programs, which involve individualized support delivered by paid assistants who are not healthcare professionals. These programs typically offer at least 20 hours of assistance per week to individuals living in the community. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of personal assistance for children and adolescents with physical impairments. Additionally, it aimed to assess the broader impacts of personal assistance on others, in comparison to alternative interventions. To identify relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple electronic databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, ERIC, and Dissertation Abstracts International, as well as specialized Swedish databases. The search covered the period from 1980 to June 2005. Reference lists were reviewed, and 345 experts, organizations, government agencies, and charities were contacted to locate pertinent research. The review focused on children and adolescents aged 0 to 18 years with physical impairments who live in the community and require assistance with daily living tasks, such as bathing and eating, or participation in normal activities due to permanent impairments. Only controlled studies were considered, specifically those in which participants were prospectively assigned to study groups and where outcomes for the control group were measured concurrently with those of the intervention group. Two reviewers independently screened the titles and abstracts of identified studies. A total of 130 full-text papers were examined in detail. However, none of the studies met the inclusion criteria for this review. As a result, no eligible studies were identified. The authors concluded that research in this area is currently limited. They suggested that when new personal assistance programs are implemented, recipients could be randomly assigned to different forms of assistance to facilitate comparative research. While personal assistance is often supported for various reasons, this review highlights the need for further studies to determine which models of personal assistance are most effective and efficient for specific populations.
